title: Predicting Consequences and Reinforcing Navigation Policies with Latent World Models
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Aug 2026]
    Title:Predicting Consequences and Reinforcing Navigation Policies with Latent World Models
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:World models enable agents to reason about future outcomes and learn policies from their knowledge of state transition, but existing approaches primarily focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits their effectiveness for decision making. In this work, we propose a compatibility prediction Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations. Our key insight is that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity, enabling action consequences to be evaluated directly in latent space. To support counterfactual training, our model leverages action sequences sampled across trajectories and learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the learned world model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning entirely within the world model. This imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance. The code, pretrained models, and additional materials are available at this https URL.

report.summary: A latent world model for robot navigation predicts feature compatibility to evaluate actions, enabling policy learning from unlabeled video and imagination-driven RL without annotations.
report.background: World models help agents reason about future outcomes, but existing approaches often reconstruct future observations or features, which adds unnecessary complexity. This paper introduces a compatibility-prediction latent world model (LWM) for robot navigation. Instead of reconstructing observations, the model predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility, exploiting the insight that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity. Action consequences are thus evaluated directly in latent space. To enable counterfactual training, the model samples action sequences across trajectories and learns which sequences lead closer to the goal. This allows policy learning from unlabeled video, followed by reinforcement learning entirely within the model. The framework removes the need for action annotations and extra environment interaction. Experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show substantial gains over prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance.
key_points: Instead of reconstructing future observations, LWM predicts latent feature compatibility. This reduces complexity and focuses on decision-relevant information. Spatial proximity is tied to feature similarity, so evaluating action consequences directly in latent space is efficient. This design avoids unnecessary reconstruction overhead.

The model supports counterfactual training by sampling action sequences across trajectories. It learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. This means learning can occur from unlabeled video data without requiring action annotations, lowering data collection costs.

The learned world model supervises policy learning from unlabeled video, then refines policies through reinforcement learning entirely within the model. This imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for additional environment interaction, enabling safe and fast policy iteration inside a simulated latent space.

Experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show significant improvements over prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance. Code and pretrained models are publicly available for validation and extension.
report.impact: This work shifts world models from observation reconstruction to goal-oriented latent prediction, making them more scalable and data-efficient. For the AI industry, it means robots and autonomous agents can learn from the massive amount of unlabeled video already available, reducing the need for expensive labeled datasets and real-world trial-and-error. Developers can accelerate training pipelines by using the model as a simulated environment, iterating policies without physical risk. For regular users, this could lead to more adaptable and reliable navigation in home assistants, delivery robots, and autonomous vehicles. The principle of latent compatibility may also inspire new approaches in other sequential decision-making domains, from manipulation to autonomous driving.
report.tools: Watch the official code repository and pretrained models linked on the arXiv page (or via CatalyzeX/alphaXiv). For comparisons, explore latent world model libraries like DreamerV3, and navigation simulators such as Habitat and Isaac Sim to benchmark real-world transfer. The paper's method can be integrated with standard RL frameworks like Stable-Baselines3 for policy learning.
